headline: Cautions that buyers moving from residential to commercial need to first understand the asset class, ensure SMSF investment strategy is documented, and maintain sufficient liquidity and managed-fund support alongside any property holding
reasoning: Wayne Bemet notes that many investors are attracted to commercial property (e.g. industrial warehouses) as residential becomes less attractive, but the first question he asks clients is 'why?' He emphasises that SMSF holders often lack a formal investment strategy and risk over-concentrating in a single illiquid asset. He argues that a managed investment (equities/managed fund) should act as the 'support act' to provide liquidity alongside the property holding. He also observes that Australian equity markets are near all-time highs despite significant policy noise, suggesting equities are being overlooked unnecessarily.
quote: My first question is why? You know, certainly there's going to be more media around this in the future, but why do they want to do it? Are they doing it because it seems easier on the surface potentially. But also if they have an SMSF, how does this actually fit in with their investment strategy? Because a lot of people with SMSF don't necessarily have a dedicated investment strategy for their fund... if you don't have a support act as in enough liquidity in your fund from cash holdings as well as a supporting app from a managed fund, because a lot of people are overlooking the markets at the moment as well. You know, there's a lot of noise around markets when we haven't been that far from all time highs.
episode_title: Why commercial property needs more than a good yield | the advisory

headline: CBD office yielding ~8.5% but vacancy at ~16% — a COVID hangover with decentralised workforce risk; chasing the yield is dangerous given structural oversupply
reasoning: CBD office space in Australia is carrying approximately 16% vacancy, which Bemet characterises as a COVID hangover reflecting the shift to decentralised workforces. Landlords are being forced to lower prices while simultaneously trying to charge inflated rents, creating an unsustainable tension. The 8.5% yield being advertised in some markets is elevated precisely because the underlying asset risk is elevated. Investors attracted to the headline yield without understanding vacancy dynamics face significant concentration and income risk.
quote: The biggest thing that people can kind of fall into is chasing yield. For example, I think we've got office space around CBDS at around about a 16% vacancy rate, whereas small industrials are around about 3%. So that's telling a very clear story that although people like the idea of maybe having a CBD office space, the, you know, 8 1/2% yield, that's kind of being floating around, it's up there for a reason because the properties and they are cheaper for a reason because I think it's a bit of a COVID hangover, decentralised workforce as well. So they're having to lower their prices in the office spaces, but also trying to get people to plan, pay inflated rent. So, you know, it can be a risky thing around, you know, chasing that sort of yield.
episode_title: Why commercial property needs more than a good yield | the advisory

headline: Government removal of CGT negative gearing for new builds has muddied the residential investment proposition, creating mass confusion among mum-and-dad investors
reasoning: The Australian government's budget night decision to remove CGT negative gearing for new builds has disrupted the traditional residential property investment thesis. This has created widespread confusion among retail investors about where to allocate capital, what grandfathering rules apply, and whether government policy is deliberately engineering a property valuation correction to improve affordability. Wayne Bemet sees clients scrambling for clarity on their position in the investment cycle.
quote: I think the Australian investor is looking for something a little bit different because as you know, on budget night, government decided to remove CGT negative gearing for new bills, which kind of threw a spinner of the works for the traditional investor for for the Australian investor. And mum and dad's trying to get ahead outside their PPOR into an investment property. So it's in, in a sense they've muddied the investment profile and where people are kind of looking, well, where do we go now because there is a lot of noise and confusion from where what we're seeing as well.
episode_title: Why commercial property needs more than a good yield | the advisory

headline: Small industrial commercial property compelling inside SMSF structures, with ~3% vacancy versus ~16% for CBD office; focus on lease quality over capital growth
reasoning: Commercial property, particularly small industrial assets, is attracting growing interest as an alternative to residential given the policy shift. Within an SMSF, commercial property retains favourable tax treatment — CGT is roughly 10% after discounts before pension phase, much lower than the new residential burden. Small industrial vacancy is around 3%, signalling strong demand, while CBD office sits at ~16% vacancy partly due to COVID-driven decentralised workforce trends. Bemet emphasises that the investment thesis for commercial property is primarily about lease quality and tenant creditworthiness rather than capital appreciation, and investors need to treat themselves as quasi-business partners to the tenants.
quote: I think more and more people are talking about commercial property and it's an interesting one as well, particularly inside SMSF because the government has made it, although they've disincentivised residential property outside of SMSF, inside the structure of an SMSF commercial property can go quite well. You are still paying capital gains if you sell before pension age, but it's nowhere near the indexation rate. So after cuts and discounts around about 10% if you sell it before or realise that capital gain before pension phase.
episode_title: Why commercial property needs more than a good yield | the advisory
